Andy Robertson has emphasized that strengthening Liverpool's defensive solidity will be crucial if the club hopes to mount a serious challenge for the Premier League title under new manager Arne Slot. The Scottish left-back believes that the foundation of any successful championship campaign rests on a reliable backline, and he is optimistic about the early indicators from Slot's tenure. Through their first two fixtures of the season, Liverpool have managed to keep their goal untouched, a promising sign for a squad transitioning under fresh leadership. However, the real examination of their defensive resilience looms on Sunday, when the Reds travel to face Manchester United at Old Trafford. This away trip is expected to provide a far sterner challenge than their opening encounters, where both Ipswich Town and Brentford failed to find a way past the Liverpool rearguard, helping Slot get off to an ideal beginning in his managerial role at Anfield.

Handle on defensive matters has clearly been a focal point of conversations within the squad, particularly when reflecting on last season's shortcomings. During the previous campaign, Liverpool conceded 41 goals across their 38 league matches as they ultimately settled for a third-place finish. That tally was significantly higher than the totals posted by the top two finishers—seven more than eventual champions Manchester City, and a striking 12 more than runners-up Arsenal. These statistics illustrate just how much defensive ground Liverpool needed to make up if they wanted to seriously contend for the title. Robertson acknowledged this reality candidly, noting that the team's early performances under Slot have given supporters genuine reasons for optimism. "I think in the first two games, you've seen that, two clean sheets, which we couldn't have asked for better," the defender remarked, expressing hope that the team can sustain this defensive discipline moving forward, including against Manchester United and the various opponents awaiting them after the upcoming international break.

Reflecting further on the previous season's disappointments, Robertson offered an honest assessment of where Liverpool fell short compared to their title rivals. He pointed out that even during periods when the team remained genuinely in contention for the championship, they were allowing opponents more scoring opportunities than both Arsenal and Manchester City were permitting. According to the Scotland international, this tendency to concede chances was always going to catch up with them eventually, and that is precisely what unfolded over the course of the campaign. Robertson's analysis suggests that the squad has internalized these lessons and recognizes that limiting opposition chances must become a defining characteristic of their play if they wish to push for silverware this term under their new head coach.
